title: Marketing Education in the Age of Generative AI: Preparing Graduates for Human–AI Collaboration
venue: Academy of Marketing Marketing Education SIG white paper
extended_summary:
This white paper examines how generative AI is reshaping marketing education and what that means for curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, employability, ethics, and institutional policy. The central problem is not whether AI should be used, but how educators can integrate it in ways that preserve disciplinary learning, critical judgement, transparency, and ethical accountability. The paper argues that GenAI has become a normal condition of both student learning and marketing practice, and that education must shift from focusing on output production to evaluating, directing, and justifying AI-assisted work.

The paper draws on three sources of evidence: a review of contemporary literature, the experience and expert contributions of the Academy of Marketing Marketing Education Special Interest Group development team, and an online survey of 89 marketing educators conducted in September–October 2025. The survey sample was predominantly UK-based and included educators teaching undergraduate and postgraduate programmes. The paper uses these inputs to identify where GenAI is changing teaching most strongly, especially in branding and communications, customer insight and analytics, and strategic decision-making.

Across the paper, the authors recommend redesigning learning around process visibility and human-led reasoning. Suggested practices include AI-use disclosure, prompt and version logs, critique of AI outputs, verification checklists, reflective commentary, and oral defences. The paper concludes that effective marketing education should embed AI within core modules, strengthen staff capability in judgement-led pedagogy, support equitable access, and align policy with teaching design. It positions GenAI as a collaborator that can support creativity and efficiency, but only when human expertise remains responsible for interpretation, contextualisation, and ethical judgement.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a sector white paper and literature synthesis with a convenience survey of 89 educators, not a controlled empirical study. It provides useful descriptive insights but does not meet criteria for rigorous causal evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful but unquantified educational and institutional effects, especially for curriculum redesign and assessment practices. Because the evidence is descriptive and no effect sizes are reported, the observed impact is best classified as modest or unclear rather than clearly large.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI used as a co-creator and feedback partner in marketing education, including chat-based prompting for brainstorming, drafting, refinement, critique, and iterative comparison of AI-generated outputs against human-revised work.

AI-generated formative feedback and critique on student marketing outputs, especially through compare-and-improve tasks, prompt/version logs, verification checklists, and revision cycles that surface reasoning rather than only final products.

finding.finding_summary: This white paper reports survey findings from n=89 marketing educators and synthesizes literature on curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, employability, and governance. The evidence indicates broad perceived institutional disruption from GenAI, alongside calls for structural redesign of policy and assessment rather than simple prohibition or detection-based control. No causal effect sizes are reported because the paper is a sector white paper and not an intervention study.
finding.measure: Survey perceptions of institutional readiness, curriculum/assessment change, and governance needs; literature synthesis
finding.study_size: n=89 (survey); broader literature review not specified

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can support critical thinking, reflection, and judgement when students are required to critique, refine, and justify outputs, but may also erode deep reasoning through cognitive offloading and over-reliance. Evidence is qualitative and conceptual, informed by survey responses (n=89) and cited classroom accounts rather than a controlled impact estimate.
finding.measure: Perceived development or erosion of critical thinking, metacognition, and judgement in marketing tasks

finding.finding_summary: Across marketing curriculum areas, educators report that GenAI can improve ideation, scenario testing, branding, analytics interpretation, and strategic comparison, but can also produce generic, stereotyped, or strategically flawed outputs that weaken disciplinary understanding if used uncritically. The paper provides no experimental effect size; it relies on survey perceptions (n=89) and examples of classroom use cases.
finding.measure: Perceived changes in marketing curriculum learning and disciplinary reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly notes that GenAI accelerates drafting, brainstorming, feedback cycles, and workflow orchestration in marketing education and practice. This is presented as a practical benefit rather than a quantified causal effect; no effect size or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived productivity, drafting speed, and workflow efficiency in AI-supported tasks
